_meta.note: Phase 2 golden set. All entries reviewed and verified by the author on 2026-08-02 per CLAUDE.md rule 6. Renamed 'draft_answer'/'draft_citation' retained as field names for now; content reflects reviewed answers.

questions.question: How would you determine whether a room qualifies for the home-office deduction?
questions.draft_answer: Under IRC §280A(c)(1), a portion of a home qualifies if it is used exclusively and on a regular basis as (A) the principal place of business for a trade or business, (B) a place used by patients/clients/customers to meet with the taxpayer in the normal course of business, or (C) (for a separate structure) in connection with the trade or business.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Explain how the principal-place-of-business test applies to a taxpayer who works both from home and at client locations.
questions.draft_answer: A home office can be the principal place of business even if the taxpayer also performs services elsewhere, provided the home is used for the administrative or management activities of the business and there is no other fixed location where substantial administrative or management activities occur.
questions.draft_citation: IRC §280A(c)(1)(A); Pub. 587, Principal Place of Business
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Describe how the home-office deduction is calculated using actual expenses.
questions.draft_answer: Determine the business percentage of the home (e.g., by square footage), allocate indirect expenses (utilities, insurance, general repairs, depreciation) by that percentage, and deduct direct expenses (benefiting only the business area) in full. The result is subject to the gross-income limitation under §280A(c)(5).
questions.draft_citation: Pub. 587, Figuring the Deduction — Actual Expenses; IRC §280A(c)(5)
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: What does 'exclusive use' mean for purposes of the home-office deduction?
questions.draft_answer: The specific area of the home is used only for the trade or business; any personal use, even incidental, disqualifies it, except for statutory exceptions (inventory/product-sample storage, and daycare facilities under §280A(c)(4)).
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: What does 'regular use' mean for purposes of the home-office deduction?
questions.draft_answer: The area is used for business on a continuing basis, not merely occasionally or incidentally — sporadic business use does not satisfy the requirement even if that use is otherwise exclusive.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: A taxpayer uses 200 square feet of a 2,000-square-foot home exclusively and regularly for business. Using the area method, what percentage of indirect home expenses is potentially allocable to business use?
questions.draft_answer: 200 / 2,000 = 10% of qualifying indirect expenses, before applying the §280A(c)(5) business-income limitation.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: A taxpayer has $12,000 of qualifying indirect home expenses and uses 15% of the home for business. Before applying any income limitation, how much is allocated to the business portion?
questions.draft_answer: $12,000 × 15% = $1,800, before applying the §280A(c)(5) limitation.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: A taxpayer begins using a qualifying office on July 1. How should part-year business use affect the home-office calculation?
questions.draft_answer: Under the simplified method, allowable square footage is averaged over the months of qualifying use (0 sq ft Jan–Jun, actual sq ft Jul–Dec, divided by 12), per Pub. 587's worked examples. Under actual expenses, deductions and depreciation are similarly limited to the qualifying period.
questions.draft_citation: Pub. 587, Using the Simplified Method — Example 1
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Distinguish between deductible business mileage and nondeductible commuting expenses.
questions.draft_answer: Commuting — travel between home and a regular/main place of business — is a nondeductible personal expense. Business mileage is travel between business locations (e.g., between job sites, from a regular workplace to a client, or, if home qualifies as the principal place of business under §280A, from home to another work location in the same trade or business).
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Compare the standard-mileage method with the actual-expense method.
questions.draft_answer: The standard mileage rate (70 cents/mile for 2025) substitutes for actual operating costs and depreciation and must be elected in the vehicle's first business-use year; the taxpayer then can't also deduct actual operating expenses (parking/tolls/some loan interest remain separately deductible). The actual-expense method requires tracking real costs allocated by business-use percentage.
questions.draft_citation: Pub. 463, Standard Mileage Rate; Actual Car Expenses
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: What records should a taxpayer maintain to substantiate business use of a vehicle?
questions.draft_answer: Under §274(d) and Treas. Reg. §1.274-5: (A) the amount of the expense/mileage, (B) the time and place of the use, (C) the business purpose, and (D) the business relationship of any person involved, substantiated by adequate records or sufficient corroborating evidence.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: What information should generally be included in a contemporaneous mileage log?
questions.draft_answer: Date of trip, odometer readings or total miles, destination, and business purpose — recorded at or near the time of the trip rather than reconstructed later.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: A taxpayer drives every morning from home to a permanent office and returns home at night. Are these miles deductible?
questions.draft_answer: No — absent a qualifying home office, travel between home and a regular/permanent place of business is nondeductible commuting, regardless of distance.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: A taxpayer drives 20,000 total miles during the year, of which 8,000 are documented business miles. What percentage of vehicle use is business use?
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: A taxpayer using actual expenses has $9,000 of eligible vehicle operating expenses and 40% business use. Before considering other limitations, how much is allocated to business use?
questions.draft_answer: $9,000 × 40% = $3,600, before other limitations (e.g., depreciation caps).
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Describe how a sole proprietor reports business income and ordinary business expenses.
questions.draft_answer: Gross receipts, cost of goods sold (if applicable), and ordinary and necessary business expenses under IRC §162 are reported on Schedule C (Form 1040), arriving at net profit or loss.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Explain how Schedule C income flows through to Schedule SE.
questions.draft_answer: Net profit (or loss) from Schedule C, line 31, is carried to Schedule SE, where (subject to minimum thresholds) it becomes the starting point for net earnings from self-employment and self-employment tax.
questions.draft_citation: Schedule C Instructions; Schedule SE Instructions
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Describe how self-employment tax is calculated for a sole proprietor.
questions.draft_answer: Net earnings from self-employment are multiplied by 92.35% to get the SE tax base, which is then subject to 12.4% Social Security tax (up to the annual wage base, $176,100 for 2025) plus 2.9% Medicare tax (uncapped, with an additional 0.9% surtax above certain thresholds, computed separately on Form 8959).
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: What is the general distinction between gross receipts, gross profit, business expenses, and net profit on Schedule C?
questions.draft_answer: Gross receipts: total income before reductions. Gross profit: gross receipts minus cost of goods sold (if applicable). Business expenses: ordinary and necessary operating costs under §162. Net profit: gross income minus total business expenses — the figure that flows to Schedule SE.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: A freelance designer receives payments through cash, checks, credit cards, and a payment application. Which payments are potentially included in Schedule C gross receipts?
questions.draft_answer: All of them — gross receipts include all income received for services regardless of payment method, including amounts that may not be separately reported on a 1099-K or 1099-NEC.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: A consultant earns $80,000 of gross business income, incurs ordinary business expenses, uses a qualifying home office, and drives documented business miles. Explain the order in which these items affect Schedule C net profit and how the resulting amount relates to Schedule SE.
questions.draft_answer: Gross receipts less ordinary §162 expenses and vehicle expense yields tentative profit; the home-office deduction (subject to the §280A(c)(5) income limitation, computed after other business deductions) is then applied to reach Schedule C net profit (line 31), which is the figure carried to Schedule SE, multiplied by 92.35% and taxed at 12.4%/2.9% subject to the SS wage base.
questions.draft_citation: Schedule C Instructions; IRC §280A(c)(5); Schedule SE Instructions; IRC §1401
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: What does IRC §280A(c)(1) require for the home-office exception to the general disallowance rule?
questions.draft_answer: Exclusive and regular use as (A) the principal place of business, (B) a place for meeting patients/clients/customers, or (C) (for a separate structure) in connection with the business.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: What four elements does Treas. Reg. §1.274-5 require to substantiate a vehicle expense under §274(d)?
questions.draft_answer: Amount, time and place (or date/description), business purpose, and the business relationship of the person involved.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Under §1401, net earnings from self-employment are first multiplied by what percentage before the combined SE tax rate applies?
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Per the 2025 Schedule SE instructions, what is the maximum amount of self-employment income subject to social security tax?
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Per Publication 463, what is the 2025 standard mileage rate for business use of a car?
questions.draft_answer: 70 cents ($0.70) per mile.
questions.draft_citation: Pub. 463 (2025), What's New — Standard mileage rate
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Under the simplified method in Publication 587, what is the prescribed rate per square foot and the maximum allowable square footage?
questions.draft_answer: $5 per square foot, capped at 300 square feet (maximum $1,500 deduction).
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: What does Form 8829, Part I, ask a taxpayer to enter regarding percentage of home used for business?
questions.draft_answer: Total home square footage and business-use square footage (or daycare hours), to compute the business-use percentage carried to Part II.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: What is the combined self-employment tax rate (Social Security + Medicare) under §1401 before the wage-base cap applies?
questions.draft_answer: 15.3% (12.4% Social Security + 2.9% Medicare).
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Does the strict substantiation requirement under §274(d) apply to 'listed property,' and what does that include?
questions.draft_answer: Yes — §274(d)(3) applies the requirement to listed property as defined in §280F(d)(4); Treas. Reg. §1.274-5 implements the recordkeeping standard, with an exception for qualified nonpersonal-use vehicles.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: How does the deductibility standard under IRC §162 differ from a personal, living, or family expense?
questions.draft_answer: §162(a) allows a deduction only for ordinary and necessary expenses of carrying on a trade or business; inherently personal expenses are not deductible regardless of any business benefit — relevant directly to mixed-use costs like a home office or vehicle.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: What does Form 8829 require for allocating 'indirect expenses' versus 'direct expenses'?
questions.draft_answer: Direct expenses (benefiting only the business area) are entered in full; indirect expenses (benefiting the whole home) are entered in full then multiplied by the business-use percentage.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Per Publication 463, what is the first-year special (bonus) depreciation percentage for a vehicle placed in service after January 19, 2025?
questions.draft_citation: Pub. 463 (2025), What's New — Special depreciation allowance
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Can I claim the §199A qualified business income deduction on my Schedule C profit?
questions.draft_answer: Out of scope — QBI/§199A phase-ins and SSTB classification are explicitly excluded from this system's corpus. Correct behavior: refuse and state the limitation.
questions.draft_citation: n/a — refusal, no corpus document covers §199A
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: How much California state income tax do I owe on my self-employment income?
questions.draft_answer: Out of scope — federal tax authority only; no state tax documents are in the corpus. Correct behavior: refuse and redirect to a state-tax resource/professional.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: I'm converting my sole proprietorship to an S-corp — what tax forms do I need to file?
questions.draft_answer: Out of scope — entity structuring/conversion isn't covered by the corpus (sole-proprietor Schedule C materials only). Correct behavior: refuse.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: What's the MACRS depreciation schedule for a rental property I bought this year?
questions.draft_answer: Out of scope — real-property/rental depreciation beyond the basic vehicle-depreciation content in Pub. 463 isn't covered. Correct behavior: refuse.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: I just hired my first W-2 employee — what payroll taxes do I need to withhold and remit?
questions.draft_answer: Out of scope — employer payroll-tax withholding is distinct from self-employment tax and isn't in the corpus. Correct behavior: refuse.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Given my income this year, should I set up a solo 401(k) instead of a SEP IRA?
questions.draft_answer: Out of scope — retirement-plan selection requires personalized financial/tax judgment not covered by the corpus. Correct behavior: refuse and note this requires a CPA/financial advisor.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: My friend said since I use my car for work sometimes, I can deduct the entire cost of the vehicle — that's right, isn't it?
questions.draft_answer: No — correct behavior is to correct the premise. Only the business-use percentage of vehicle costs is deductible; occasional work use does not make the full cost deductible.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: My accountant said as long as I occasionally work from my living room, I can deduct my full mortgage payment as a home-office expense — correct?
questions.draft_answer: No — the space must be used exclusively and regularly for business; occasional use of a shared living space fails the exclusive-use test, and even a qualifying office only supports a proportional allocation, not the full mortgage payment.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: I already pay income tax on my freelance income, so self-employment tax doesn't apply to me too — right?
questions.draft_answer: No — self-employment tax is separate from and in addition to federal income tax; it applies to net earnings from self-employment regardless of income tax owed.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: I don't need a mileage log if I'm confident in my year-end estimate — that's fine for the IRS, isn't it?
questions.draft_answer: No — §274(d)/Treas. Reg. §1.274-5 require substantiation by adequate records or sufficient corroborating evidence made at or near the time of the expense; a year-end estimate doesn't meet this standard.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Does Publication 463's MACRS depreciation percentage for a given recovery year differ for a car placed in service in 2022 versus one placed in service in 2025?
questions.draft_answer: Potentially yes — the chart is keyed to the placed-in-service year; a taxpayer uses the chart/column for that year throughout the recovery period. Check whether the ingested Pub. 463 (2025 edition) actually contains the 2022 chart or only 2025 — this may expose a real corpus gap worth reporting as a known limitation.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Does the fair-market-value threshold used to figure the lease-inclusion amount differ for a lease beginning in 2021 versus one beginning in 2024?
questions.draft_answer: Yes — per Pub. 463's lease-inclusion FMV table, thresholds vary by year the lease began (e.g., $51,000 for 2021 vs. $62,000 for 2024–2025).
questions.draft_citation: Pub. 463, Leasing a Car — FMV table
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Does the 2025 standard mileage rate in Publication 463 apply to a return for a different tax year, or is each year's rate published separately?
questions.draft_answer: Each tax year has its own published rate; 70 cents/mile is specific to 2025 and should not be applied to a different year. [Also tests whether the system flags that the ingested corpus mostly only contains the 2025 rate — a known limitation if it fails to catch this.]
questions.draft_citation: Pub. 463 (2025), What's New — Standard mileage rate
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: Does the $176,100 Social Security wage base for SE tax apply to a calculation for a different tax year, or does that threshold change annually?
questions.draft_answer: The wage base is indexed and changes annually, published each year in the Schedule SE instructions' What's New section; $176,100 is specific to 2025.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: A taxpayer's net profit from self-employment is $150,000. What is the SE tax?
questions.draft_answer: Net earnings = $150,000 × 92.35% = $138,525. Since this is below the $176,100 wage base, full amount is subject to 12.4% SS (≈$17,177.10) + 2.9% Medicare (≈$4,017.23) ≈ $21,194 total SE tax.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: A taxpayer's net profit from self-employment is $200,000. What is the SE tax, given the 2025 wage base?
questions.draft_answer: Net earnings = $200,000 × 92.35% = $184,700. SS portion applies only up to $176,100 → ≈$21,836.40. Medicare applies to the full $184,700 → ≈$5,356.30 (before the separate 0.9% additional Medicare surtax on Form 8959). Total ≈ $27,193.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: A taxpayer uses 350 sq ft exclusively and regularly for business. Using the simplified method's cap, what is the maximum deduction?
questions.draft_answer: The simplified method caps allowable area at 300 sq ft, so the deduction is limited to 300 × $5 = $1,500, even though 350 sq ft is actually used.
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: A home-office deduction is limited by the business-income limitation, reducing Schedule C net profit further than it otherwise would be. How does that reduced figure flow through to the Schedule SE calculation?
questions.draft_answer: The home-office deduction is limited to roughly the gross income from business use of the home after other deductions (§280A(c)(5)); any disallowed excess carries forward. The net profit actually reported on Schedule C line 31 (after the limitation) is what's carried to Schedule SE — so the limitation indirectly increases net profit (and SE tax) relative to full allowance.
questions.draft_citation: IRC §280A(c)(5); Schedule C Instructions; Schedule SE Instructions
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: A taxpayer's home office qualifies as their principal place of business, and they also deduct mileage for trips from home to client sites. Does claiming that mileage affect the 'regular and exclusive use' test for the home office?
questions.draft_answer: No — Pub. 587 explicitly notes that if the home office qualifies as principal place of business, daily transportation costs between home and other work locations in the same trade or business are deductible; this doesn't itself violate exclusive use, since that test looks at how the office space is used, not the taxpayer's travel patterns.
questions.draft_citation: Pub. 587, Tip under More than one place of business; IRC §280A(c)(1)
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: A taxpayer used the standard mileage rate in year one, then switches to actual expenses (with depreciation) in year three. How does the earlier election constrain the depreciation method available, and how does that flow into Schedule C net profit feeding Schedule SE?
questions.draft_answer: Pub. 463 requires straight-line depreciation for the vehicle's remaining useful life if standard mileage was used in the first business-use year (accelerated MACRS isn't available after that). The resulting straight-line depreciation is one component of actual vehicle expenses reducing Schedule C net profit, which carries to Schedule SE.
questions.draft_citation: Pub. 463, Depreciation Deduction — Methods of depreciation; Schedule C/SE Instructions
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.

questions.question: A taxpayer's home-office deduction is capped by the income limitation in one year, carrying over disallowed expenses. How does that carryover interact with a switch to the simplified method the following year?
questions.draft_answer: Per Pub. 587, a disallowed actual-expense carryover cannot be deducted in a year the taxpayer uses the simplified method — it continues to carry forward and can only be used again in a future year the taxpayer returns to the actual-expense method.
questions.draft_citation: Pub. 587, Using the Simplified Method — No deduction of carryover of actual expenses
questions.review_notes: Reviewed and verified by author on 2026-08-02.
